candidates.title: Anchor numeric error-code patterns in log-tail monitors to avoid substring false positives
candidates.evidence: A background Monitor watching a live pipeline's driver+server logs raised a false alarm on an HTTP '529' error; the actual log line contained an unrelated microsecond timing value ('...1529µs') whose digits happened to contain the substring '529'. The agent had to stop, diagnose the false positive, and rewrite the grep pattern with boundary anchoring (require whitespace/'in' context, exclude periodic heartbeat lines) to avoid repeat false alarms that risked the Monitor auto-stopping from event flooding and losing visibility into the real long-running job.
candidates.novelty: Baseline's Tooling and Operational Safety section covers distinguishing I/O-wait hangs from real failures and reading raw provider logs instead of coarse signals, but says nothing about numeric substring collisions when building error-detection regexes over streamed/tailed logs.
candidates.principle: When writing a regex to flag error/status codes (e.g. HTTP status) in streamed or tailed logs for a background monitor, anchor the match to field boundaries (preceded by whitespace or a labeled key, not preceded/followed by other digits) rather than a bare substring search. Unrelated numeric fields in the same log line -- timings in µs/ms, byte counts, ids, ports -- can contain the same digit sequence, and an unanchored pattern produces false alarms that waste investigation time or can trip an event-flood auto-stop on a long-running watch.
candidates.placement: guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md (or a Tooling and Operational Safety addition) -- the section governing background Monitor/task-notification use

candidates.title: Separate 'move processing downstream' from 'drop raw fields' when lightening a data pipeline
candidates.evidence: Asked to redesign a usage-data collector to be 'lighter and more robust,' the agent proposed dropping fields it judged unused/dead as part of the redesign. The user corrected: '기존 정보량 대비 변경된 설계에서 정보량이 줄어들면 안돼. 우리는 프로세싱을 서버에서 하려는거지, 정보량을 줄이려는거아니야' (the goal was moving processing to the server, not shrinking captured information), forcing the agent to redo the design so raw signal was fully preserved and only derived/interpretive computation moved downstream.
candidates.novelty: Baseline's Concept Economy and Coding Guidelines cover keeping scope narrow and deriving values from source authority, but do not name this specific conflation risk in pipeline-lightening work: treating 'currently unused field' as license to drop raw capture, versus the intended move of only relocating computation.
candidates.principle: When asked to make a data-collection/normalization pipeline lighter or more robust, keep two moves explicit and separate: (a) relocating derived/interpretive processing to a stage that can already (or will) compute it downstream, and (b) removing raw fields because they look currently unused. Do (a) freely. Treat (b) as a distinct, materially different decision requiring explicit confirmation -- 'no current consumer reads this' is not evidence the raw signal is worthless, since raw retention preserves future reprocessing and analysis options that a derived value cannot recover.
candidates.placement: CLAUDE.md Coding Guidelines or guides/coding-staged-workflow.md (design-stage guidance for pipeline/schema redesigns)

candidates.title: Diagnose 'command not found' for known-good binaries as a PATH-stripped network wrapper first
candidates.evidence: curl and python3 both reported 'command not found' inside a verification script. The agent first suspected sandbox restrictions and disabled sandboxing (no fix), then tried exporting PATH explicitly (still no fix), before discovering the actual cause: commands that touch the network execute inside a bare '(eval):' wrapper with an empty PATH that `export PATH` does not reach; only absolute binary paths (e.g. /usr/bin/curl) worked. Multiple diagnostic turns were spent before the correct cause was isolated.
candidates.novelty: Baseline's Tooling and Operational Safety section addresses confirming env/config reached a subprocess via a cheap artifact and not trusting coarse ps signals, but has no entry for this specific harness behavior: network-touching Bash invocations losing PATH in an eval wrapper that export does not fix.
candidates.principle: When a Bash command that performs network I/O reports 'command not found' for a binary independently confirmed to exist and be on PATH (e.g. via `which`), suspect an execution wrapper specific to network-touching commands that runs in a bare eval context with an empty PATH -- not fixed by `export PATH` -- before concluding the sandbox is blocking it. Isolate by testing the same binary in a non-network command; if that succeeds, route around the wrapper using the binary's absolute path instead of relying on PATH resolution.
candidates.placement: CLAUDE.md Tooling and Operational Safety section (a harness-level quirk that recurs across any project using this environment)

candidates.title: Attribute a parallel session's git action by tool-execution evidence, not transcript mentions
candidates.evidence: To determine which of three parallel Claude sessions created specific branches/commits, the agent first grepped all session transcripts for the commit hash and branch name. It caught its own error: '그럽이 오염되었습니다 — 메모(release-rollout-resume) 본문에 이 커밋 해시·브랜치명이 들어 있어 모든 세션 컨텍스트에 주입되므로, 단순 언급으로는 실제 작업한 세션을 못 가린다' -- because a shared handoff/memory doc loaded into every session's context contained the same identifiers, the mention-search matched every session. It then re-derived attribution from actual command executions (e.g. a literal `gh pr create --head ...` invocation) instead.
candidates.novelty: The multi-model guide's Sessions/Branches/Worktrees section covers relocation, pwd/branch/HEAD re-verification, and handoff hygiene, but has no rule for this specific transcript-forensics pitfall: shared-context pollution defeating a naive text-mention search when attributing which parallel session performed an action.
candidates.principle: When determining which of several parallel agent sessions actually performed a given git/infra action, do not attribute by grepping transcripts for mentions of the identifying token (commit hash, branch name, resource id) -- any handoff, resume note, or memory file loaded into multiple sessions' context will inject the same tokens into every one of them and produce matches everywhere. Attribute instead from evidence of actual execution -- the literal command invocation and its result in that session's own transcript -- not textual co-occurrence.
candidates.placement: guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md, Sessions/Branches/Worktrees section

candidates.title: Check baked config file permissions against a container's non-root runtime UID
candidates.evidence: A freshly built and deployed gateway container failed to boot with 'open /config/gateway.meta.json: permission denied'. Root cause: the signing tool wrote meta.json/evidence.json with 0600 permissions; the image runs as non-root UID 65532, so the root-owned 0600 files baked in via COPY were unreadable at runtime (a sibling file at 0644 booted fine). Fixed by changing the tool's output permissions to 0644 and rebuilding -- a full extra build-deploy-diagnose-rebuild cycle for a class of bug invisible at build time.
candidates.novelty: Baseline has no coverage of container file-permission / non-root-UID interactions for baked artifacts anywhere in Tooling and Operational Safety or the Coding Guidelines' verification menus.
candidates.principle: When a build step generates or signs files that get baked into a container image running as a non-root user, check the emitted files' permission bits before trusting the image will boot -- a generator or signing tool that defaults to owner-only permissions (0600) silently produces a root-owned, non-root-unreadable file once COPY'd in, and the failure only surfaces at container start, not at build time. Require the tool to emit permissions the runtime UID can read (typically 0644), or explicitly chmod after COPY, and verify this as part of the image build check rather than only at first live boot.
candidates.placement: guides/coding-staged-workflow.md Verification Menus (code domain) -- container/deploy artifact checks

candidates.title: Verify the active cloud CLI project/context matches intent, not just git state
candidates.evidence: Resuming a saved checklist to re-run a full test pass, the agent found the ambient `gcloud` active project was `d1-ai-dashboard` while the intended target from the checklist was `day1-ai-dashboard-dev`, and flagged this mismatch before running any command: '엉뉱한(혹시 prod) 프로젝트에 배포하지 않도록 먼저 확인이 필요합니다.' It then pinned every subsequent gcloud invocation with an explicit --project flag for the rest of the session rather than mutating or trusting the global default, avoiding a risk of acting against production infrastructure.
candidates.novelty: Baseline's cli-multi-model-workflow guide has an explicit rule for git-state drift ('re-verify pwd; in a repo, branch and HEAD... against the pinned handoff') but nothing for cloud CLI (gcloud/aws/kubectl) active-context drift, which carries an equal or greater blast-radius risk -- a wrong-environment deploy or teardown -- and the same silent-ambient-default failure mode.
candidates.principle: Ambient CLI context for cloud tools (active gcloud project, aws profile, kubectl context) drifts across sessions and unrelated work in exactly the way git branch/HEAD does, and using it implicitly before an environment-affecting command (deploy, IAM change, teardown, resource creation) risks acting on the wrong environment. On session resume, or before the first resource-affecting command of a session, explicitly diff the active cloud context against the intended target; if they differ, do not switch the global default -- pin the target explicitly on every command for the rest of the session (--project/--profile/--context) instead.
candidates.placement: CLAUDE.md Tooling and Operational Safety section, as a sibling bullet to the existing git pwd/branch/HEAD verification rule; or guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md Halt And Resume section

candidates.title: grep silently misdetects non-ASCII-heavy source files as binary, giving a false 'no match'
candidates.evidence: This exact failure recurred at least four times in the batch: session d64ecafd needed 'grep -a' to find a match in a UTF-8 file; session 6b5ffea5 found grep returned exit 1 (no match) on a .ts file with many Korean comments while `git diff` plainly showed the line was present, and the agent had to fall back to Read to confirm; session 9f75d597 hit a grep failure attributed to zsh globbing and switched to ripgrep; session d66cb116 again logged 'grep 도구가 이 파일에서 비정상입니다. 직접 읽겠습니다.' and fell back to a direct Read. In each case the agent burned a turn diagnosing before working around it, and in one case only caught the false negative because an independent source (git diff) contradicted it.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's Tooling and Operational Safety section covers confirming tool flags/versions empirically and treating coarse runtime signals (ps reads, failure labels) as hypotheses to verify against low-level evidence, but it has no rule about grep's binary-detection heuristic misfiring on legitimate non-ASCII text files, which is a distinct and recurring failure class in this corpus (a silent false negative, not a crash or flag error).
candidates.principle: Treat a no-match/failure result from `grep` on a source file with heavy non-ASCII content (e.g. non-English comments) as a hypothesis, not proof of absence: grep's binary-detection heuristic can misclassify such UTF-8 files as binary and silently return no matches instead of an error. When a grep miss contradicts another source of evidence (git diff, a prior read, a teammate's report), re-run with a flag that forces text mode (e.g. `grep -a`) or use a tool that does not binary-sniff (e.g. ripgrep) before concluding the pattern is absent.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md, Tooling and Operational Safety section — as a sibling bullet to the existing 'ps env read is unreliable' rule, since both are about not trusting a coarse tool signal without corroboration.

candidates.title: Resource-creation CLIs can echo secret values into their own success output
candidates.evidence: While registering scheduler jobs with a bearer-token secret injected as a shell variable (not typed literally), the agent found that the cloud CLI's job-creation command echoed the full created job configuration — including the secret header value — back to stdout, exposing the secret in the session transcript. The agent flagged this mid-session as a security issue it could not have prevented by variable injection alone, and advised treating the transcript as compromised.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's secrets rule ('Never accept secrets through transcript- or history-logged channels; provide a gitignored env slot, read the value only from the environment... advise rotating anything already pasted') addresses secrets flowing IN (typed/pasted by a human or model). It does not address secrets flowing OUT: a tool's own response to a legitimate, variable-injected creation call can itself contain the secret in plaintext, which is a different leak direction with a different mitigation (suppress/redact the echoed output, or treat any resource-creation call that accepts a secret payload as a rotation trigger).
candidates.principle: When a tool call creates or updates a resource whose payload includes a secret (a token, key, or credential), assume the command's own success output may echo that secret back verbatim — even when the secret was passed via a variable rather than typed literally — because some CLIs and APIs return the full resource state on creation. Redirect or suppress such output where possible, and treat any secret that was passed through a command whose output you did not fully control as exposed: rotate it, the same as a pasted secret.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md, Tooling and Operational Safety section — as a companion bullet to the existing secrets-input rule, extending it to cover secrets leaking through a command's own output.

candidates.title: Prove the downstream consumption path before flipping an irreversible collection switch
candidates.evidence: Before redeploying a gateway to turn on sensitive-data capture (an action described as hard to reverse and one that changes the system's data-collection posture), the agent explicitly ordered the work as: first build and validate the decryption/consumption tool against already-existing sealed records from a prior brief capture window, prove it can read what was captured, and only then perform the irreversible production redeploy that turns capture back on — reasoning '켜고 나서 못 읽으면 곤란하니까요' (no good turning it on if you can't read it afterward).
candidates.novelty: The baseline's default-off/opt-in rule for risky changes ('Land risky or behavior-changing work behind a default-off path... enabled by an explicit opt-in, so the change stays reversible') covers making the change itself reversible via a flag, but this session's switch was inherently costly to leave off-then-on (each activation window collects data you cannot get back if you can't read it). The distinct, more specific practice — validate the consumer/decoder path against existing or historical samples before activating an irreversible collection step — is not stated.
candidates.principle: Before activating a costly-to-reverse data-collection, capture, or side-effect switch, first build and verify the downstream consumption path (decoding, decryption, parsing, or analysis) against existing or historical samples of that data. Only flip the switch once you have proven you can actually use what you are about to collect — otherwise a successful activation can still be a wasted or unrecoverable window.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md, Coding Guidelines section — adjacent to the existing 'land risky work behind a default-off opt-in path' bullet, as a refinement for switches whose activation itself (not just the code) is hard to reverse.

candidates.title: Survey and catalog prior-art failure modes empirically before designing into an existing space
candidates.evidence: Before designing an expanded tool-coverage surface, the user directed the agent to dispatch parallel agents against roughly ten existing open-source implementations in the same space, extract their actual tool/coverage designs from source, and explicitly catalog which patterns to adopt and which documented failures (e.g. exposing a raw passthrough operation) to avoid repeating — saving the result as a reusable prior-art failure study before writing the new design, which then explicitly designed against the cataloged failure ('passthrough is the very trap we ruled out').
candidates.novelty: The coding-staged-workflow guide's high-level design stage lists goal/scope/architecture/tradeoffs/completion-criteria but does not mention surveying external prior art or cataloging competitor failure modes as part of design; the multi-model guide's fan-out patterns cover independent workstreams generically but not this specific competitive-analysis-before-design step.
candidates.principle: When designing a system in a space with existing implementations, empirically survey a representative sample of those implementations (via parallel search/extraction agents, not memory), catalog their documented or observable failure modes explicitly, and design against those failures by name. Persist the survey as a reusable document so later design decisions can be traced back to a specific prior failure being avoided, rather than an unstated preference.
candidates.placement: coding-staged-workflow.md guide, Stage 1 (High-level design) — add prior-art survey and failure cataloging as an optional input to the design stage when comparable systems exist.

candidates.title: A single run cannot verify a probabilistic mechanism — repeat the probe to measure a failure rate
candidates.evidence: After building and validating a falsifiable test harness (confirmed to pass on a faithful mock and fail on a broken mock), the agent ran the real LLM-backed mechanism once, observed a failure, and then explicitly re-ran it five more times specifically to measure a failure rate rather than stopping at the single result — arriving at a quantified 2/6 (~33%) failure rate that shaped the design conclusion, at a token cost the agent confirmed was negligible before running.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's verification-proportionality rule says to 'probe at N=1 with inputs precondition-checked' before expensive live runs, which is framed for cost-gating a single confirmatory probe. It does not distinguish the case where the mechanism under test is itself non-deterministic (LLM-driven): for such mechanisms a single pass or single fail is not a reliable verdict, and the corpus shows this session explicitly recognized that and paid for repeated trials to get a rate instead of a binary verdict.
candidates.principle: When probing a mechanism whose behavior includes LLM-introduced non-determinism, do not conclude soundness or failure from a single real-probe result. After the harness itself is validated with cheap negative controls, budget for a small number of repeated real trials (roughly 5-6) of the same probe to estimate a failure rate, and report that rate rather than a single pass/fail — a lone run can both understate and overstate a probabilistic mechanism's true reliability.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md, Verification Discipline section — as a refinement to the existing 'probe at N=1' bullet under proportional verification, scoped specifically to mechanisms with LLM/probabilistic non-determinism.

candidates.title: Pin exact handle/session id when polling concurrent async review jobs
candidates.evidence: Mid-session the agent polled a 'latest' review-session selector to check its own design review and got back results from a different, unrelated concurrent review session (target 'internal') because another review had started more recently. It caught the mismatch itself, switched to the exact session id, and re-polled correctly — costing an extra round of investigation before the real results were read.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's cli-multi-model-workflow.md says 'Idle/progress notifications are hypotheses; verify repo artifacts before re-dispatch' and 'Resume-first from artifacts that parse... and match their recorded fingerprint', which cover verifying resumed state, but nothing addresses the specific 'latest' selector failure mode where a convenience filter silently resolves to a different concurrent job's output rather than the caller's own.
candidates.principle: When polling a long-running or async job by handle, avoid 'latest'/most-recent convenience filters once more than one such job can be in flight at the same time (parallel reviews, parallel builds, shared queues) — pin and re-use the exact id/handle returned at dispatch time, since 'latest' can silently resolve to a different concurrent job and produce plausible-looking but wrong results.
candidates.placement: guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md, Delegation Mechanics And Teammate Persistence or Halt And Resume section

candidates.title: Shell pipeline exit code reflects only the last command, not earlier failures
candidates.evidence: While validating a data-parity check built from a piped shell command, the agent explicitly flagged that the pipeline's exit code came back 0 even though an earlier stage in the pipe was the one that mattered ('exit code도 확인하고(파이프라인 때문에 0으로 나옴)') — catching that the exit status could not be trusted as-is before drawing a conclusion from it.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's Verification Discipline section says to trust a green check only when it traversed real dispatch and calls, and to be suspicious of unexpectedly fast/empty green results, but it never names the concrete pipe-exit-code masking mechanism (only the last command's status survives a shell pipe unless pipefail is set) as a specific thing to check before trusting a shell-based verification step.
candidates.principle: When a shell pipeline's exit code is used as a pass/fail verification signal, remember it reflects only the last command by default — enable pipefail or check each stage's exit code explicitly, because an early failing command can be masked by a later successful one and produce a false-green result.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md, Verification Discipline section (or Tooling and Operational Safety)

candidates.title: Pass shell-metacharacter prompts (e.g. a literal $ skill name) via stdin, not as a CLI arg
candidates.evidence: When dispatching a cross-CLI skill invocation whose name began with a literal '$', the agent explicitly chose to inject the prompt via stdin specifically to avoid shell expansion of the '$' ('프롬프트는 stdin으로 주입($ 셸 확장 회피)'), and repeated the same stdin-injection pattern for a later dispatch in the same environment.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's cli-multi-model-workflow.md documents Codex direct-drive flags, sandbox/approval defaults, and dispatch packets in detail, but does not mention shell-metacharacter escaping as a dispatch-mechanics concern; this is a distinct, concrete technique not covered.
candidates.principle: When invoking a CLI with a prompt or argument string that may contain shell metacharacters (a literal $, backticks, quotes, or a tool/skill name with a special prefix), pass it via stdin or a file rather than as a raw command-line argument, so the shell does not expand or mangle it before the target process sees it.
candidates.placement: guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md, Driving Codex CLI Directly section

candidates.title: A bare 'check memory for next task' is ambiguous across multiple tracked repos/workstreams
candidates.evidence: Asked only to check memory for the next task, the agent picked a specific pending item from one repo and began verifying/planning it (several turns of real WIP investigation); the user then had to interrupt and explicitly redirect to a different, unrelated task in a different repo entirely ('docs_create는 우리 작업이 아니야... 브랜치와 워크트리가 맞는지도 확인해야 해'), pointing to separate memory files to establish the correct track.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's cli-multi-model-workflow.md says to re-verify pwd/branch/HEAD against a pinned handoff after any resume, which addresses confirming state within a chosen track, but not the earlier ambiguity of *which* track/repo to choose when a memory index spans multiple independent, simultaneously-active workstreams across different repos.
candidates.principle: When a memory or handoff index tracks multiple independent workstreams — especially across different repos or worktrees — treat a bare 'check memory / what's next' request as ambiguous rather than defaulting to the most salient or most-recently-touched entry; confirm which specific workstream and repo is meant before investigating or starting work, since guessing can lead to real (if reversible) work in the wrong track.
candidates.placement: guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md, Sessions, Branches, Worktrees or Halt And Resume section

candidates.title: Blind counterbalanced multi-persona LLM judges for subjective product decisions, checked for confounds
candidates.evidence: To decide whether a page-layout variant actually improved persuasion (no objective ground truth available), the agent ran two rounds of blind matched-pair comparison with multiple distinct target-customer personas as judges, counterbalancing which variant was labeled A vs B across judges to null out position bias. After round 1 came back 8/8 in the variant's favor, the agent itself discovered a confound (the baseline's images were empty placeholder stubs, not the real content) that could have explained the result, then reran a second, decisive round with the confound removed before trusting the 6/6 convergent verdict.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's review-request.md guide covers evidence bars, severity, and verdict shape for code review specifically, and the mock-realization guide covers mock-vs-real completion credit, but neither addresses the distinct pattern of using blind, position-counterbalanced, multi-persona LLM judges to evaluate a subjective product/UX quality question, nor the specific discipline of checking test-fixture parity (missing/placeholder assets) for confounds before trusting a comparative verdict.
candidates.principle: For subjective or qualitative product-quality decisions with no direct ground-truth metric (persuasion, aesthetics, tone, UX variety), evaluate with blind matched-pair comparisons across multiple distinct judge personas, counterbalancing which option is labeled first/A across judges to cancel position bias; before trusting the result, verify both compared artifacts are rendered/populated equivalently (no missing assets or other fixture asymmetry), since an unintended difference in fixture fidelity can masquerade as the effect under test.
candidates.placement: guides/coding-staged-workflow.md, Verification Menus (add a product/UX decision row) or global CLAUDE.md Verification Discipline section

candidates.title: A teammate's 'idle' notification can arrive without its result ever having been reported
candidates.evidence: Across one session, multiple spawned teammate agents (used as parallel research/review workers) sent an 'idle, available' notification with no accompanying result message on several separate occasions; each time the agent had to notice the absence of a report and explicitly ask the teammate to send it before the actual findings arrived, including at least one case where a duplicate idle notification arrived after the report had already been received.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's cli-multi-model-workflow.md already says 'Idle/progress notifications are hypotheses; verify repo artifacts before re-dispatch', which covers not blindly re-dispatching on a false idle signal, but does not cover the distinct, repeatedly-observed failure mode where idle and result-report are decoupled events that can arrive in either order (or duplicated) — requiring an explicit ask for the report rather than treating idle as completion.
candidates.principle: Treat a teammate/subagent's idle-or-available notification as independent of whether it has actually delivered its result — idle can arrive before, after, or duplicated relative to the report. If idle arrives with no attached report, explicitly request the report rather than assuming none is coming or that the unit is simply done.
candidates.placement: guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md, Delegation Mechanics And Teammate Persistence section

candidates.title: Diagnose shared-quota stalls via account-wide concurrency, not just the current job's own
candidates.evidence: Investigating why a serial, single-concurrency production LLM batch job intermittently hit single-call timeouts, the agent measured account-wide process concurrency (including unrelated sibling sessions sharing the same provider account) at each stall timestamp against a no-stall baseline window, found stalls correlated with higher account-wide concurrency from other sessions, and reported the finding together with an explicit correction to its own earlier hypothesis.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's Unattended Batch Safety section covers circuit breakers and backoff once a limit is hit, and the Tooling section covers treating coarse signals as hypotheses to be confirmed against authoritative evidence, but neither names the specific diagnostic technique of correlating intermittent shared-quota failures against total concurrent usage across all sessions/processes on that account (not just the job under investigation), using a negative-control time window.
candidates.principle: When diagnosing intermittent stalls or timeouts under a quota or rate limit shared across sessions/processes, do not judge the cause only from the current job's own concurrency — measure total concurrent usage across everything sharing that quota at the failure timestamps and compare against a no-failure baseline window before attributing the cause.
candidates.placement: guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md, Unattended Batch Safety section

candidates.title: ISO timestamp string comparison breaks silently across producers with differing precision
candidates.evidence: During a multi-round adversarial cross-verification of a data-retention design (ultracode find + onto independent review + codex re-verify + direct code grounding), a load-bearing rule compared event timestamps as strings. A later verification round discovered that one producer emits timestamps without milliseconds ('...56Z') and another emits them with milliseconds ('...56.789Z'); because '.' (0x2E) sorts before 'Z' (0x5A) in ASCII, mixed-precision timestamps compare out of true chronological order under plain string comparison. This was confirmed against production data (mixed precision within the same session) and required switching the comparison to a real timestamp type (`::timestamptz` cast) — it survived to a second cross-verification round as a still-open high-severity finding (Q1) even after the first fix pass.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's llm-capability-boundary-patterns guide discusses grounding/provenance and timestamp-like fields only as 'runtime-owned' metadata, and the coding guidelines mention 'root cause' and 'single-source the value' generally, but nowhere calls out the specific, recurring class of bug where multi-producer ISO-8601 timestamps compared as raw strings silently misorder when precision (millisecond presence) differs across producers. This is a concrete, reusable data-correctness gotcha absent from the baseline.
candidates.principle: When ordering or comparing timestamps sourced from more than one producer/system, never compare them as raw strings — parse them into a real datetime/timestamp type before comparison. String-lexicographic comparison of ISO-8601 timestamps silently misorders whenever producers differ in precision (e.g., presence or absence of milliseconds), because punctuation and letter characters used as precision delimiters do not sort chronologically; verify this specifically whenever a design's core decision axis is 'newest wins' across heterogeneous event sources.
candidates.placement: Coding Guidelines section of global CLAUDE.md (near the 'fix the root cause at its authority' bullet), or a new bullet in the llm-capability-boundary-patterns.md 'Runtime-Owned Deterministic Fields' section since timestamp comparison often backs a provenance/recency field.

candidates.title: Allowlist config can pass boot checks yet silently deny a whole route class on key-format mismatch
candidates.evidence: A live production tool gateway denied every request for an entire class of grouped tools (13 tools) with tool_not_allowed. Root cause: the config listed grouped tools by bare name (e.g. 'sheets_structure') while the gate compares against a composite per-action RouteKey ('sheets_structure:add_sheet'); the mismatch meant the config passed boot/deploy validation (no boot-time check verifies allowlist entries resolve against the live route table) but denied every actual request. The fix required correcting every entry to its RouteKey form, re-signing the config, redeploying, and validating with an explicit negative control (old config denies, new config allows, an intentionally-excluded scope still denies) plus a live E2E call through the redeployed gateway before declaring done.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's llm-capability-boundary docs cover validator/schema/enum single-source-of-truth drift and runtime-owned fields, but do not name this specific, high-consequence pattern: an authorization/allowlist config whose entries must match a runtime-constructed composite key, where a format-mismatched entry (bare name vs. composite key) is invisible to boot-time validation and silently blocks 100% of the affected route class at request time. This is a distinct, generalizable operational-safety gap not covered by existing 'schema drift' or 'grounding' rules.
candidates.principle: When a permission/allowlist config's entries must match a key the runtime constructs at request time (e.g., a composite 'resource:action' key for grouped routes vs. a bare name for flat ones), add a boot-time or deploy-time check that resolves every configured entry against the live route/gate key space — do not rely on schema-shape validation alone. candidates.title: Verification and gate code should fail loud on unexpected shape, not silently fall back
candidates.evidence: The session's own schema-verification script used a defensive fallback, `s.$defs || s.definitions`, to read a JSON Schema key. Because the actual schema was draft-07 (key `definitions`, no `$defs`), the fallback silently absorbed the mismatch and the script kept passing, masking that a citation in the design pointed at a nonexistent key. An independent reviewer caught it, and the session confirmed: '제 확인 스크립트가 $defs || definitions 폴백을 써서 조용히 넘어가는 바람에 못 봤습니다' (my check script used a $defs||definitions fallback and silently passed over it, so I missed it).

candidates.principle: When writing verification, audit, or gating code that inspects a schema, config, or artifact for a specific field or shape, assert the expected key/shape explicitly and fail loudly if it is absent, rather than reaching for a permissive fallback (`a || b`) across plausible alternatives. candidates.title: Clear language/test caches between rapid mutate-then-test cycles in mutation testing
candidates.evidence: While building defect-witness tests via mutation testing (sed-mutate a value on disk, cp/restore, run pytest, repeat), the digest shows: 'sed/cp/pytest가 1초 안에 실행돼 pytest의 assertion-rewrite 캐시(mtime+size 기준)가 무효화되지 않은 것' — the on-disk value was already restored to the correct value but pytest's assertion-rewrite cache (keyed on mtime+size) hadn't invalidated within the same second, so it reported a stale failure. The agent explicitly flagged this as invalidating all prior mutation results ('앞선 변이 검사 결과는 신뢰할 수 없습니다') and had to clear the cache and rerun all 10 mutations plus the baseline before trusting any of them.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's Verification Discipline section (global CLAUDE.md) has strong rules about trusting green checks only over real dispatch, and about falsifiable/mutation-style controls ('prefer signals that fail when the mechanism is wrong'), but nothing addresses that the test tool's OWN caching layer can silently invalidate a mutation-testing loop by reusing stale compiled/rewritten bytecode when file mutations happen faster than the cache's mtime/size resolution. Searched baseline for 'cache', 'mutation', 'mtime', 'stale' — all 'cache' hits are about LLM prompt caching (a different concept entirely); no hit addresses local build/test tool caches. This is a genuinely absent, tool-level gotcha distinct from the existing data-freshness/provenance-staleness rules (which are about source documents, not local test infrastructure).
candidates.principle: When running a rapid mutate-file → run-test → restore-file loop (mutation testing, defect-witness verification, or any tight edit-then-verify cycle), do not trust results at face value: many test/build tools cache compiled or rewritten artifacts keyed on file mtime+size (e.g. pytest's assertion-rewrite cache, bytecode caches, incremental compiler caches), and mutations executed within the same timestamp-resolution window as the prior run can silently reuse stale cached output instead of re-processing the mutated file — producing a result that looks like a real pass/fail but reflects the previous file state. Either clear the relevant tool cache before each iteration in such a loop, insert a cache-busting delay/flag, or use a tool invocation mode that disables caching, and re-verify the baseline (unmutated) case still passes after clearing the cache before trusting any mutation result from that loop.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md, Verification Discipline section — as a new bullet adjacent to the existing 'Trust a green check only when it traversed the actual changed code through the real dispatch and real calls' bullet, since it is the same trust-the-check-only-when-warranted family but targets a different failure mode (tool-level cache staleness rather than mock/dry-run substitution).

The agent had to diagnose this explicitly ('전부 100% → 차이 없음이 아니라 구분 불가'), redesign the fixture around a different difficulty axis (reasoning depth / cross-file causal chains mined from real review findings, not just bug subtlety), before the full 45-run batch was worth running. candidates.title: Snapshot persisted state before an in-place resume/overwrite of a completed run

A downstream failure during the resume — even one unrelated to the resume logic itself, such as a billing/quota rejection surfacing many layers later as malformed data — can otherwise corrupt or destroy the only copy of completed work, and restoring from the snapshot may be the only clean recovery path.

candidates.title: Rule out pre-existing CI failure before debugging a local-pass/CI-fail gap as a regression
candidates.evidence: The local test suite (including -race) was fully green after the redaction/recover change, but the gateway PR's CI 'test' job kept failing. Many turns went into hypotheses (module cache staleness, -race-specific timing, go.mod verify, SDK source inspection of tool-name validation) before checking whether the same CI job also failed on the commit immediately preceding this session's change — it did, on multiple prior commits, which reclassified the failure as pre-existing and environment-specific (CI linux/amd64 vs local darwin/arm64) rather than caused by the diff.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's verification rules (Verification Discipline) describe when to trust a green result (real dispatch, non-mocked) but say nothing about efficiently triaging a CI-only FAIL against a locally-green change. Closest existing rule (git-fetch-before-diff) addresses a different failure mode (stale local base), not this one.

If it did, the failure predates the diff and is very likely an environment difference (OS/arch, cache, toolchain flag) rather than something the change caused — investigate that gap first, not the diff.
candidates.placement: coding-staged-workflow.md Verification Menus (Code), or a new bullet in the global Tooling and Operational Safety section near the existing git-fetch-before-diff rule

candidates.title: Add a cache/idempotency guard to any auth-minting path an unattended loop can call repeatedly
candidates.evidence: The user reported 100+ OAuth authentication windows open after leaving the computer running unattended overnight. Root cause: an unattended overnight cross-verification batch's tool-discovery path minted a fresh auth token on every call with no cache, producing 103 real prompts over about 50 minutes — the exact defect class the day's planned architectural fix (a catalog cache) was designed to close.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's existing circuit-breaker rule (Unattended Batch Safety) triggers on provider limit/auth/transport *failures*, halting after repeated failed attempts. It does not cover a code path that succeeds on every call but lacks a cache — a failure-triggered breaker never fires because nothing fails, yet the loop still floods the user with real side effects at loop frequency.
candidates.principle: Before running any unattended or overnight agent loop or batch, check whether it repeatedly invokes an auth-minting, token-issuing, or other real-side-effect-triggering code path with no cache or idempotency guard. A call that succeeds every time is not covered by failure-based circuit breakers, yet it can still flood the user with real side effects (e.g. authentication prompts) at loop frequency. Add a cache or idempotency guard to that path, or bound the loop's call rate to it, before leaving it unattended.
candidates.placement: cli-multi-model-workflow.md Unattended Batch Safety section, as an addition alongside the existing failure-triggered circuit breaker

candidates.title: Compact the cross-session memory index before it exceeds its read-size limit, preserving index-only detail first

Before compacting to one-line-per-topic summaries, the agent checked whether any detail existed only in the index (not duplicated in a per-topic file), found one such case, migrated it out first, then compressed the index and confirmed every link still resolved and no topic file was left orphaned.

candidates.principle: The cross-session memory index has a read-size limit; if it grows past that limit, a future session silently receives a truncated index and loses information with no error. Periodically check the index's size, and before compacting it into one-line-per-topic summaries, verify whether any detail exists only in the index and not in a per-topic file, migrate that detail out first, then confirm every index link still resolves and no topic file is orphaned.
candidates.placement: global Documentation Hygiene section, or a new subsection in cli-multi-model-workflow.md near Handoff Contract

candidates.title: Correct a stale memory-index 'current track' pointer in the same session that finds it, not later

candidates.principle: When the memory index's stated current track or pointer disagrees with actual repo/branch state, do not just work around the drift for this session — correct the index's pointer before ending the session. candidates.placement: global Documentation Hygiene section, alongside the index size-limit rule from the companion candidate

candidates.title: Upgrade major dependencies in isolated, verified layers; pin runtime-coupled packages to the deploy target
candidates.evidence: A batch dependency update was grouped into risk-ordered layers with a full typecheck/lint/test gate run after each layer. Two major bumps (a lint plugin whose bundled dependency called an API removed by the new major version despite peer ranges technically allowing it, and a language toolchain major version incompatible with a downstream type-checking plugin's peer range) were independently caught as breaking and reverted without affecting the other successful layers. Separately, a type-definitions package was pinned to the version matching the production container's runtime major version rather than 'latest' or the higher version installed on the local development machine, confirmed empirically from the deployment config.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's rule to confirm a dependency version empirically covers verifying a version claim, but not the layered-isolation upgrade strategy for multiple simultaneous major bumps, nor the specific case of pinning a runtime-coupled package to the deployment target instead of the local machine or 'latest'.
candidates.principle: When bumping several outdated dependencies including major versions, upgrade in independent, risk-ordered layers and run the full verification gate (typecheck/lint/test) after each layer; a failing layer is isolated and reverted on its own rather than bisected across many simultaneous bumps. For packages whose correctness is coupled to a specific runtime (type-definition packages, engines constraints), pin the version to the actual deployment target's runtime version — confirmed from the deployment config — not to 'latest' and not to the local development machine's version, which can silently differ from production.
candidates.placement: coding-staged-workflow.md Verification Menus (Code), or a new bullet under the global Coding Guidelines

candidates.title: zsh does not word-split unquoted variables by default — probes written for bash silently misbehave
candidates.evidence: A shell probe intended to expand a multi-token variable into separate CLI arguments produced distorted results because the active shell does not perform bash-style unquoted word-splitting by default; the agent had to explicitly separate the arguments to get a correct probe result.
candidates.novelty: No shell-specific guidance exists anywhere in the baseline. This is a distinct failure mode from the covered runtime-signal and probe-verification rules: the script does not error, it silently returns a plausible but wrong result.
candidates.principle: Do not assume bash's unquoted-variable word-splitting when writing shell probes or scripts. A common default shell (zsh) does not split an unquoted variable into multiple words by default, so a probe expecting `$var` to expand into several arguments will silently pass it as one argument instead of erroring. Confirm the active shell and use explicit splitting (arrays, or literal separate arguments) rather than relying on default word-splitting behavior.
candidates.placement: global Tooling and Operational Safety section

candidates.title: unref/close stdio on a child process spawned for a one-shot CLI health check to avoid an event-loop hang
candidates.evidence: A new health-check CLI command spawned a subprocess to probe status, printed the correct result, but the parent process never exited because the spawned child's process handle (and its open stdin) kept the runtime's event loop alive. The fix was to unref the child process and destroy its stream handles once the probe result was captured.
candidates.novelty: The baseline's spawn-related guidance is entirely about spawning LLM subagents/CLI agents for delegation (When To Spawn, Delegation Mechanics); it does not address OS-level child-process lifecycle management within a single tool's own runtime.
candidates.principle: When a CLI command spawns a child process purely to run a bounded health or auth probe and should then exit, explicitly unref the child process and close or destroy its stdio handles once the result is captured. An un-unref'd child, or an open stdin pipe to it, keeps the runtime's event loop alive and makes an otherwise-successful one-shot command hang instead of exiting.
candidates.placement: No clear existing home in the current guide structure; would be a narrow addition to the global Coding Guidelines or a runtime-specific note if one is created

candidates.title: Untracked new files are invisible to git-diff-based review tools
candidates.evidence: The agent noted new component files were untracked and therefore invisible to the git-diff-based review harness ('새 컴포넌트 파일들이 untracked라 git diff 기반 리뷰 하네스에 안 잡힙니다'), and had to use git add with intent-to-add to bring them into the diff before dispatching the Codex cross-verification review (built-in code-review, level high).

candidates.principle: Before dispatching a git-diff-based review (built-in code-review, cross-family verification, PR review), confirm new/untracked files are included in the diff scope — stage them (e.g. with git add --intent-to-add) first, since a diff-based reviewer silently skips untracked files and would return a 'clean' verdict without ever having seen them.
candidates.placement: guides/review-request.md or coding-staged-workflow.md's Review Loop — alongside the existing 'read participation before believing a verdict' rule, as another mechanism by which a review can be silently non-authoritative.

candidates.title: git diff two-dot notation is a direct snapshot diff, not a commit-range exclusion like git log
candidates.evidence: The agent used origin/main..HEAD to diagnose a branch and misread unrelated file deletions (src/mcp/*, README, package.json) as part of the current change; it later determined this was because the branch's merge-base predated a separate upstream merge (#192), so those files' absence from the old branch showed up as apparent deletions in the two-dot diff, explicitly flagged as '오해의 소지' (misleading) once re-diagnosed via the actual merge-base.
candidates.novelty: Baseline's Tooling and Operational Safety section already has a git-fetch/range rule about computing origin/<base>..HEAD instead of a stale local ref, but that rule addresses staleness of the LOCAL ref requiring a fetch, and is phrased for commit-range use (git log semantics). It does not state that git diff's two-dot notation behaves differently from git log's — for diff it is a direct tip-to-tip snapshot comparison, not limited to commits unique to one side — so even a freshly fetched origin ref can produce a misleading diff when the branch's merge-base is behind the target.
candidates.principle: When diffing a branch against its target for review or PR purposes, remember that git diff A..B is a direct snapshot comparison between two tips (unlike git log/git rev-list two-dot ranges, which exclude common history). If the branch's merge-base may be behind the target, use three-dot git diff A...B (diff from the merge-base) so changes made independently on the target since divergence do not appear as spurious additions/deletions on the branch.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md, Tooling and Operational Safety section — as a follow-on to the existing git-fetch/origin-base rule, since it is the same class of git-range footgun but for diff rather than log.

candidates.title: The Read tool renders NUL bytes as blank space, hiding byte-level differences
candidates.evidence: The agent needed to confirm two key-separator expressions used an identical � separator, and explicitly noted 'the Read tool renders NUL as a space,' so it verified the match via a byte-level check rather than trusting the rendered file content it had visually inspected.
candidates.novelty: Nothing in the baseline addresses this specific rendering limitation of the file-reading tool. The closest general rule ('confirm it empirically against the live or installed artifact,' Tooling and Operational Safety) is about not trusting docs/memory for versions/capabilities, not about a specific tool's display fidelity for non-printable bytes.
candidates.principle: The file-reading tool cannot faithfully display non-printable bytes (e.g. NUL) — it can render them as blank/space, visually indistinguishable from an actual space character. When byte-exact equality of separators, encodings, or binary content is load-bearing, verify with a byte-level check (hexdump/od, or a script comparing raw bytes) instead of trusting the tool's rendered text.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md, Tooling and Operational Safety section, as a tool-fidelity caveat next to the existing 'confirm empirically' rule.

candidates.placement: guides/cli-multi-model-workflow.md, Handoff Contract section.

candidates.title: Clear or verify smoke-test-only limiting config before a declared full-scale run

candidates.title: Recognize stale absolute-versioned plugin paths as a silent-breakage signature
candidates.evidence: In this session, a statusLine command in settings.json pointed at a plugin path pinned to an old version directory (1.26.1) that no longer existed on disk (actual installed version was 1.29.0), so the feature the user wanted (context-window display) was silently broken even though 'it looked configured'. candidates.placement: guides/coding-staged-workflow.md (or a new note under the global Tooling and Operational Safety section) — this is a distinct silent-failure signature from the existing runtime-signal-is-a-hypothesis rule and warrants its own recognition line.

candidates.title: Prefer verbatim section slicing over parse-and-reserialize when provisioning secrets-bearing user config
candidates.evidence: While designing MCP-server provisioning into an isolated config home, the session explicitly rejected adding a TOML parser dependency and rejected parsing+reserializing the user's config.toml, choosing instead to slice the allowlisted [mcp_servers.*] sections verbatim from the raw text — reasoning that reserialization risks losing or mutating user-defined formatting and embedded env secrets, and that a new parser dependency violates the project's zero-runtime-dependency stance. The slicer was then validated against real config shapes (single server, multiple servers, multi-subtable-plus-.env, hyphenated names, missing-key detection) before being trusted.
candidates.novelty: Baseline's Coding Guidelines say to build the smallest viable path and avoid unnecessary abstractions, and 'when exactness ... matter, use tools/code' — but there is no rule specifically about preferring byte-verbatim raw-text extraction over parse-and-reserialize when the source config may contain secrets, comments, or exact formatting that reserialization could silently corrupt. No guide mentions TOML/config reserialization risk or verbatim slicing as a technique.
candidates.principle: When provisioning a subset of a user's existing structured config (TOML/YAML/INI/JSON with comments) into another environment or consumer, prefer verbatim raw-text extraction of the relevant section over parsing the whole file and re-serializing a subset — parse-then-write risks silently dropping comments, formatting, or secret values, and can require adding a new parser dependency for a narrow use case. Validate the extraction against the range of real shapes it must handle (single entry, multiple entries, nested sub-tables, unusual key names, missing keys) before trusting it in the provisioning path.
candidates.placement: guides/coding-staged-workflow.md Coding Guidelines section, near the 'smallest viable functional path' and dependency-avoidance guidance — or a new bullet under the global Coding Guidelines about config/secret handling.

candidates.title: Verify concurrent-writer status before concluding an edit to a shared live config file was lost
candidates.evidence: After unioning mcpServers across two global Claude Code config files (~/.claude.json and ~/.claude/.claude.json), a post-edit diff showed unrelated top-level fields had also changed versus the pre-edit backup, which looked like unintended data loss from the edit. Rather than assuming corruption, the session ran a live observation window and confirmed the file's mtime changed during that window (another running Claude Code session was concurrently rewriting it) while the target mcpServers field remained correctly unioned — concluding the apparent diff was caused by a concurrent writer's normal cache/counter updates, not data loss from the edit.
candidates.novelty: Baseline's Tooling and Operational Safety rule to treat a coarse runtime signal as a hypothesis and confirm cause against authoritative low-level evidence is framed around process/CPU/log signals (hangs, pre-dispatch rejection), not around editing a config file that other live sessions concurrently rewrite. The concrete recognition — that a global settings file shared by multiple running agent sessions can show an unrelated diff purely from a concurrent writer, and this should be checked via a short live observation before concluding an edit caused data loss — is a distinct, absent case.
candidates.principle: Before concluding that an edit to a shared state/config file caused data loss or was reverted, check whether another live process (e.g. a second running agent session) also writes that file; if so, a before/after diff can show unrelated changes purely from concurrent writes. Confirm by watching the file over a short live window (mtime plus the specific field you changed) rather than treating a single before/after comparison as proof, and scope any 'union' or 'fix' to only the fields you intend to change so concurrent unrelated writes are not mistaken for or masked by your edit.
candidates.placement: global CLAUDE.md Tooling and Operational Safety section, as an addition alongside the existing 'coarse runtime signal is a hypothesis' rule — same epistemic pattern, new domain (shared config files vs. process/log signals).

candidates.title: Preserve the identity of connected cloud documents

Edit it in place through its native authority unless the user explicitly requests a clone; before writing, inventory identifiers, scripts, triggers, permissions, protections, named ranges, validations, and external links, then verify that external loads are complete and distinguish loading, timeout, quota, network, permission, and broken-reference states.
candidates.placement: Coding Guidelines → connected cloud documents and spreadsheets

candidates.title: Normalize model prices before comparing providers
candidates.evidence: A promotional student-credit equivalence was initially used to convert credits into dollars and was then explicitly retracted because it was not a general purchase rate. The comparison only became defensible after fixing the billing surface and units: direct API, standard processing, context tier, text tokens, and separate input, cache-hit, and output prices; accepted-output cost was identified as the practical benchmark metric.

candidates.title: Minimize production-data exposure during diagnostic probes
candidates.evidence: A production question involved records that could contain sensitive payloads. Instead of printing payload bodies, the session ran an explicitly scoped read-only job that returned only structural aggregates—record counts, entry counts, and whether argument fields existed—then deleted the temporary job after the decision was made.
candidates.novelty: The baseline protects secrets in transcript-logged channels but does not define a data-minimizing pattern for probing production records that may contain personal or otherwise sensitive content.
candidates.principle: When a production-data probe may touch personal, secret, or customer content, answer the question with server-side structural aggregation whenever possible: return only counts, types, key presence, bounded metadata, or hashes, never raw payloads. Scope the probe read-only, target the environment explicitly, suppress sensitive fields from logs, and remove temporary probe resources afterward.
candidates.placement: Tooling and Operational Safety → production-data diagnostics

candidates.title: Verify both mounts and latent volume definitions after secret rotation
candidates.evidence: A secret update correctly mounted the new revision but left an older unmounted volume definition in the live service template. A subsequent rotation again left the immediately previous definitions behind. Only an explicit removal step followed by readback of the newest revision made both the volume and mount lists clean.
candidates.novelty: The baseline says to verify live artifacts and consumer wiring, but it does not capture the merge-not-replace behavior of deployment update flags or the distinction between active mounts and stale secret-volume definitions.
candidates.principle: Assume managed-service update flags may merge configuration rather than replace it. After secret or volume rotation, inspect the newest live revision's volume definitions and volume mounts separately, explicitly remove every unmounted obsolete definition, and re-read the revision after any cleanup update before declaring drift resolved.
candidates.placement: Tooling and Operational Safety → cloud deployment and secret-rotation hygiene

candidates.title: Digest-verify every release channel after publication
candidates.evidence: The release used assets-first and manifest-last publication and appeared successful, yet post-publication hashing found two object-storage installers still had older bytes while the signed manifest, local staging directory, and release-host assets agreed. The objects were re-uploaded and the complete hash loop was rerun; the embedded updater was also exercised without an explicit manifest argument.
candidates.novelty: The baseline has a generic atomic-persistence and checksum pattern, but it does not cover multi-channel release publication where a signed manifest, object storage, release hosting, and the installed updater can diverge independently.
candidates.principle: For a multi-channel release, upload immutable assets before publishing the manifest, but never treat ordering as proof. After publication, verify every manifest-referenced object byte-for-byte or by digest against the staged artifact, verify release-host assets independently, and run the real updater or installer through its default discovery path; repair any mismatch and rerun the full verification matrix from the beginning.
candidates.placement: Verification Discipline → release and distribution verification

candidates.title: Require positive human provenance when mining main-context sessions
candidates.evidence: An initial Codex allowlist admitted 227 sessions, but only 20 intersected the observed human history and 195 were marked as automation. Later checks also found background sessions and history-missing sessions that defeated broader positive rules. The design was repeatedly revised so history became an independent observation rather than an oracle and ambiguous, background, automated, or provenance-missing sessions were quarantined.
candidates.novelty: The baseline contains extensive multi-agent execution guidance but no rule for classifying stored AI sessions as directly handled human main contexts rather than dispatched, automated, or background work.
candidates.principle: When mining AI-session logs for human main-context learnings, do not infer provenance from transcript existence, history membership, or broad message-shape heuristics alone. Require positive human-origin evidence plus negative checks for dispatch, automation, task, review, and background origins across independent metadata sources; treat history as an observation rather than an oracle, and quarantine ambiguous or provenance-missing sessions instead of promoting them.
candidates.placement: New session-distill guide → census and provenance classification

candidates.title: Distinguish admission throttling from quota exhaustion
candidates.evidence: The failure was initially attributed to shared usage quota. The user corrected the diagnosis: quota remained available, only additional concurrent process creation failed, a delayed or serialized retry succeeded, and ordinary two-to-four-way concurrency later worked again. This signature pointed to a short-window admission or startup-concurrency limit rather than depletion.
candidates.novelty: The baseline has rate-limit circuit-breaker guidance, but it does not identify the admission-throttle signature or explain that quota exhaustion and concurrent session-creation rejection need different recovery strategies.
candidates.principle: Do not label concurrent session-start failures as quota exhaustion without evidence. If quota remains available, existing work continues, new concurrent starts fail, and delayed or serialized starts succeed, classify the event as admission or startup-concurrency throttling; stop fan-out, stagger creation with bounded jitter and a circuit breaker, preserve per-item state, and probe recovery at low concurrency instead of retry-storming.
candidates.placement: Multi-Model Workflow → concurrency limits and circuit breakers

candidates.title: Own and terminate the whole subprocess group
candidates.evidence: A live model run produced its valid result quickly but the CLI never exited. Investigation showed a wrapper-to-binary child hierarchy; sending termination only to the wrapper could leave the actual server alive. The backend was changed to launch the owned server in an independent process group, close streams during shutdown, terminate only that group, and verify clean exit.
candidates.novelty: The baseline requires destructive process actions to target owned PIDs or ancestry, but it does not state the lifecycle rule needed when wrappers create child processes and terminating the wrapper alone can orphan the real service.
candidates.principle: When launching a long-lived subprocess through a wrapper, establish an owned process group or equivalent job boundary at startup. On shutdown, close owned streams, terminate that exact group rather than only the wrapper PID, wait for exit, and verify no owned descendants remain; never broaden cleanup to unrelated processes.
candidates.placement: Tooling and Operational Safety → subprocess lifecycle and cleanup

candidates.title: Separate model availability, activation, and certification
candidates.evidence: The initial answer treated the absence of a review certification as implying that the model needed separate validation for review. The user corrected this because the model was already registered without role restrictions and therefore routable through review. Subsequent investigation had to distinguish registry membership, route allowance, configured and conditional consumers, unwired helpers, and certification coverage; it also established that certification was tracked by model and role or pipeline rather than by every individual call site.
candidates.novelty: The baseline already says to verify live capabilities and not mistake an inert configuration value for runtime authority, but it does not define the distinct status dimensions needed for model inventories or warn that route availability and certification are independent claims.
candidates.principle: When inventorying an LLM or other pluggable runtime capability, report registry eligibility, route authorization, actual configured consumption, conditional or unwired consumption, and certification evidence as separate states. Never infer certification from availability, or unavailability from missing certification; state the certification unit explicitly, such as model-by-role or model-by-pipeline, rather than implying per-call-site coverage.
candidates.placement: CLAUDE.md > Multi-Model Workflow, near model binding and live-capability verification

candidates.title: Default repository tools to pinned project-local installation
candidates.evidence: A CLI was first installed globally and verified from a fresh login shell. The user then requested a rollback and repository-only installation. The replacement used a pinned local development dependency, generated package metadata and a lockfile, ignored the installation directory, removed the global command, and independently verified local execution and global absence. The session explicitly identified reproducibility as the advantage of the local approach.
candidates.novelty: The baseline has general scope and dependency-verification rules but no guidance for choosing between machine-global and repository-local CLI installation, nor for verifying that a scope migration actually removed the old command resolution path.
candidates.principle: For a CLI used by one repository, prefer a pinned project-local development dependency with a lockfile and an ignored installation directory; reserve global installation for tools intentionally shared across projects. When changing installation scope, verify both sides independently: the old command resolution path is absent and the new repository-local invocation resolves the pinned version.
candidates.placement: CLAUDE.md > Tooling and Operational Safety, under dependency and CLI installation scope

candidates.title: Protect dirty worktrees before pulling remote changes
candidates.evidence: Before pulling 97 remote commits into a worktree with four uncommitted files, the session fetched remote state, established that there were no local-only commits, compared incoming changed paths with the dirty paths, and used a fast-forward-only pull. Afterward it confirmed that the uncommitted changes were preserved and revalidated a generated HTML artifact because its source inputs had changed upstream.
candidates.novelty: The baseline already requires fetching before branch-range reasoning and using authoritative remote refs, but it does not cover pull safety with a dirty worktree, path-overlap analysis, fast-forward-only integration, or post-pull regeneration checks for derived artifacts whose inputs changed.
candidates.principle: Before pulling into a dirty worktree, fetch first, determine local-only and incoming commits, compare incoming changed paths against all staged, unstaged, and untracked paths, and stop if overlap or a non-fast-forward integration could endanger local work. Use fast-forward-only pull when applicable, then confirm the dirty state was preserved and revalidate any derived artifact whose inputs changed upstream.
candidates.placement: CLAUDE.md > Tooling and Operational Safety, adjacent to the existing fetch and remote-range rule
